newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai said lagging Hong Kong as finance centre.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai said lagging Hong Kong as finance centre.

text.p: Shanghai has far to go to match Hong Kong as an international financial centre, needing more freedom to manoeuvre and up-to-date transport and telecommunications, officials and scholars said on Wednesday.

"Although Shanghai will become an international trade and financial centre, for a long time its capabilities will be much lower than Hong Kong," said Zhang Zhongli, president of the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences.
He was speaking at a seminar on the impact on Shanghai of Hong Kong's return to China on July 1, 1997, after more than 150 years as a British colony.
"Reform of China's financial, banking and foreign trade system has been slow," he said, adding that Shanghai needed more freedom to move.

In the 1930s, Shanghai was the biggest international commercial, banking and manufacturing city in East Asia, far dwarfing Hong Kong, whose growth as a financial centre began only after the communist takeover of mainland China in 1949.

Chinese officials have sought to calm fears in Hong Kong that its importance will decline after the 1997 handover, and stressed that developing Shanghai as an international financial centre posed no competitive threat.

Taking up this theme, vice-major Zhao Qizheng told the seminar that conditions did not exist for Shanghai to be an international financial centre as China's currency, the yuan, was not yet convertible.
Like other major countries, China needed at least two major financial centres, and Shanghai and Hong Kong would complement each other after the latter's return to China, Zhao said.

Shanghai lags far behind Hong Kong in transport and communications and plans to spend 300 billion yuan ($36 billion) from 1996-2000 improving infrastructure, more than double that of the 1991-1995 period, Zhao said.

Writing in Wednesday's Shanghai Securities News, Professor Chen Biaoru of East China Normal University said the government needed to reduce control of the city's existing foreign exchange market, where the yuan exchange rate is tightly controlled by the central bank.
He said Shanghai needed an offshore banking centre to attract large volumes of capital from overseas.
Part of Shanghai's future was developing its role as China's biggest industrial city, Zhang said.

"Our exports lack competitiveness," he said. "China has huge labour resources but a limited standard of technology. The level of our exports is low, their added and processing value is low, and ability to respond to the market is limited," he said.
"The strength of China's own technology, research and development cannot meet the needs of industrialisation, and we rely heavily on foreign technology," he said.
